land.text: Anjou, 'roughly co-extensive with the diocese of Angers', a county of West Francia since the first count 'appointed: 861'

predecessors.note: The page's infobox dates the first count to 861 (Robert the Strong, 'around 861') and Fulk III's reign from 21 July 987; Cliopatria draws the county only from 990, when the Kingdom of France row starts and the West Franks row has ended (989).

land.text: Anjou and Maine, reunited with the crown when Philip of Valois was recognised as king on 1 April 1328

successors.note: The county lived on: 'In 1360, the county was raised into the Duchy of Anjou' (carried by the house-of-valois-anjou dossier from 1363). Cliopatria's County of Anjou row runs to 1332.

capitals.name: Angers
capitals.note: Infobox 'Capital: Angers'; the page gives no change.

rulers.name: Fulk III the Black (Nerra)
rulers.note: Page: 21 July 987 - 21 June 1040 (listed there as 'Fulk the Black'); the strip starts at Cliopatria's 990.

rulers.name: Geoffrey III the Bearded
rulers.note: 'Count of Anjou from 1060 to 1068' (Geoffrey II page).

rulers.name: Fulk V the Young
rulers.note: Page: 14 April 1109 - 1129; the strip ends where Cliopatria's County row ends (1125), the Angevins row taking over in 1126.

rulers.name: Charles of Valois
rulers.note: Count of Anjou and Maine 'in 1290' by marriage; died 16 December 1325.

rulers.name: Philip of Valois (later Philip VI)
rulers.note: Succession to Anjou is not described by the pages: the County page has the county reunited with the crown when Philip VI was recognised as king on 1 April 1328 and the Charles page says only that he left 'a son who would take the throne of France under the name of Philip VI'.

correction.text: The 990 shape without Saumur (until 1026) and Chinon (until 1044)

keyframe_review.note: 9,760 km2 for 990-1045: the page gives no area and calls the county 'roughly co-extensive with the diocese of Angers' (Maine-et-Loire is 7,166 km2, so the shape is generous). Two places are in the shape too early: 'Fulk surprised and took Saumur (1026)' and Chinon, which Theobald III surrendered after Nouy (the Geoffrey II page: 'he surrendered Tours with Chinon and Langeais', 1044). Loudun was held 'in fief' from the Duke of Aquitaine, undated, and is left in.

13,160 km2: Touraine (Tours, Loches, Amboise) is added. 'After the battle of Nouy on 21 August 1044 Theobald III, Count of Blois... was taken prisoner'; the County page: the victory 'assured to the Angevins the possession of the countship of Touraine'. Cliopatria draws it two years late. Vendôme, held by Geoffrey Martel 1032-1056 (Geoffrey II page), is not in this shape.

26,690 km2: Maine (Le Mans, Mayenne, Laval, Craon) and Vendôme are added. 'Count Geoffrey's taking possession of the city of Mans (shortly after 26 March 1051)' (Geoffrey II page); the County page: 'he was able to force Maine to recognize his authority in 1051'; the Maine page puts it 'in 1051 Hugh IV died and the citizens of Le Mans opened their gate to the Angevins', chronology disputed. Cliopatria draws Maine five years late. Alençon and Domfront, which Geoffrey 'seized', lie outside the shape; Vendôme's count ended in 1056 on the Geoffrey page.

13,160 km2: Maine is out (the same shape as 1046). 'William invaded Maine in force in 1063' and 'he controlled the county by the beginning of 1064'; the County page has Geoffrey Martel resisting in Maine until his death on 14 November 1060 and Robert Curthose doing homage for Maine in 1081. Cliopatria draws the loss in 1066. The County page also has Fulk IV ceding the Gâtinais to Philip I (undated, 1068-1109), which is not in the shape.

26,690 km2: Maine returns. Fulk V 'took Maine over in 1110 after the death of Elias' (Maine page; County page: 'succeeded to the countship of Maine on the death of Elias (11 July 1110)'). Cliopatria draws it in 1111; the identical polygon is the Angevins row of 1126-1146.

25,109 km2 for 1294-1325: Anjou and Maine without Touraine, as in the 1290 dowry: 'On 16 August 1290, Margaret married Charles of Valois, giving her Anjou and Maine for dowry' (County page; the Charles page: 'Charles became in 1290 the Count of Anjou and of Maine by his first marriage'). Charles's other apanages (Valois, Alençon 1285, Perche, Chartres) are not in the shape, which leaves out Alençon, Chartres and Crépy. Eleven scattered cells (lon 0.5-3.5, lat 47.0-49.3) are not explained by any page. No area on the pages.

correction.text: Anjou and Maine for 1326-1327 only; from 1 April 1328 the land is the French crown's

keyframe_review.note: 25,109 km2 for 1326-1332, the same shape. Charles died on 16 December 1325 and 'Philip VI's recognition as king on 1 April 1328 reunited the county with the crown', so the shape holds for 1326-1327 only; from 1328 the land is the crown's. The infobox lists John de Valois as ruler from 1332, which the page does not narrate; the county was raised to a duchy in 1360.

region.text: Anjou, roughly the diocese of Angers

ledger.note: 990: the county of Anjou stands as a great fief of the Capetian kingdom under Fulk III. The page lists Fulk the Black as count from 21 July 987 and the first count as 'appointed: 861'; the area was 'roughly co-extensive with the diocese of Angers'. Cliopatria draws the county from 990, after the West Franks row ends (989).

1026: Fulk takes Saumur. 'Fulk surprised and took Saumur (1026).' The page does not say from whom, so the counterpart is the unnamed lord of Saumur (confidence 1); Cliopatria's shape holds Saumur from 990.
Winter 1042-3: Geoffrey besieges Tours. 'Count Geoffrey laid siege to Tours in the winter of 1042-3' in alliance with Henry I; the zone is Touraine, held by Theobald III of Blois.
1044: Nouy ends the war for Touraine. 'After the battle of Nouy on 21 August 1044 Theobald III, Count of Blois (1039-89) was taken prisoner'.

1044: Tours, Chinon and Langeais pass to Anjou. 'He surrendered Tours with Chinon and Langeais, excluding, however, the monastery of Marmoutier'; the County page: the victory at Nouy (21 August 1044) 'assured to the Angevins the possession of the countship of Touraine', though Fulk 'did homage to the count of Blois for Touraine'. Cliopatria draws the shape from 1046.

region.text: Alençon and Domfront on the Norman marches

ledger.note: 1049: William of Normandy besieges Alençon. 'William, Duke of Normandy, besieged Alençon' in 1049-1051: the town had 'risen in support of the Count of Anjou' with Domfront and Bellême; the Geoffrey II page: 'Count Geoffrey assaulted Normandy and seized the towns of Domfront and Alençon'. The zone is not inside Cliopatria's Anjou shape.

region.text: Maine: Le Mans, Mayenne, Laval, Craon, and the Vendômois

ledger.note: 1051: Geoffrey takes Le Mans and Maine. 'Count Geoffrey's taking possession of the city of Mans (shortly after 26 March 1051)'; County page: 'he was able to force Maine to recognize his authority in 1051'. The Maine page: Hugh IV died and 'the citizens of Le Mans opened their gate to the Angevins' (chronology disputed). Cliopatria draws Maine from 1056.

region.text: Alençon and Domfront on the Norman marches

ledger.note: 1052: William retakes Alençon and Domfront. 'Duke William laid siege to Domfront, which resisted his efforts to retake it throughout the winter of 1052'; he then 'rapidly retook Alençon and then Domfront, driving Count Geoffrey back across the Norman border into Maine' (outcome corrected by reviewer eu-10-a). The Normans date the end of the campaign 1050 (taking of Passais, History of Normandy page, see the duchy-of-normandy dossier); the Mortemer invasion followed in early 1054 and Varaville in 1057.
1062: Saintonge goes to the Duke of Aquitaine. Fulk allowed Saintonge to be 'taken in 1062 by the duke of Aquitaine'. The land is not in Cliopatria's Anjou shape.

region.text: Maine: Le Mans, Mayenne, Laval, Craon, and the Vendômois

ledger.note: 1063: William of Normandy conquers Maine. 'William invaded Maine in force in 1063' and 'he controlled the county by the beginning of 1064'; Herbert II had died in 1062 naming William heir. Le Mans rose against the Normans in 1069 and expelled them in 1070 (Hugh V proclaimed count). Cliopatria draws the loss in 1066.

region.text: Maine: Le Mans, Mayenne, Laval, Craon, and the Vendômois

ledger.note: 1110: Fulk V takes Maine. He 'took Maine over in 1110 after the death of Elias' (Maine page); County page: 'succeeded to the countship of Maine on the death of Elias (11 July 1110)'. Cliopatria draws it from 1111.

region.text: Anjou and Maine, drawn from 1126 by the Angevins and the Angevin Empire

ledger.note: 1126: Cliopatria continues the county's polygon (26,690 km2) as the Angevins row to 1146 and then as the Angevin Empire to 1209 (bridging; the County page has Geoffrey V Plantagenet 1129-1151, Normandy received on 19 January 1144, Henry II recognised as king on 19 December 1154, Philip II's conquest of Anjou in 1202-1203, the appanage to Charles of Provence in August 1246 and Charles II from 7 January 1285). The county is drawn by those states until it reappears in 1290.

region.text: Anjou and Maine, the dowry of Margaret of Anjou

ledger.note: 1290: Anjou and Maine pass to Charles of Valois. 'On 16 August 1290, Margaret married Charles of Valois, giving her Anjou and Maine for dowry'; the Charles page: 'Charles became in 1290 the Count of Anjou and of Maine by his first marriage' (August 1290). The land was Charles II's, of the Capetian House of Anjou. Cliopatria draws the county from 1294.

1328: Anjou and Maine are reunited with the crown. Charles of Valois died on 16 December 1325 and 'Philip VI's recognition as king on 1 April 1328 reunited the county with the crown'. Cliopatria keeps the county to 1332 (the infobox lists John de Valois as ruler from 1332, the county 'raised into the Duchy of Anjou' in 1360).

region.text: Anjou and Maine, reunited with the crown

ledger.note: 1328: the county of Anjou is absorbed into the royal domain; the later Duchy of Anjou (1360) is carried by the house-of-valois-anjou dossier.

wars.name: Battle of Nouy
wars.outcome: Angevin victory on 21 August 1044; Theobald III of Blois captured and Tours, Chinon and Langeais surrendered.
wars.note: Geoffrey besieged Tours in the winter of 1042-3 with Henry I's help. Not dated to a month beyond 21 August 1044.

wars.name: Norman-Angevin struggle for Alençon and Domfront

zones.text: Alençon and Domfront on the Norman marches

wars.outcome: William besieged Alençon (1049-1051) and Domfront (winter of 1052); the Norman dossier has Passais taken in 1050.
wars.note: Not a Wikipedia article title; the Geoffrey II page has the winter 1052 siege of Domfront.

wars.name: Battle of Mortemer
wars.outcome: 'In late January, early February 1054, Count Geoffrey and King Henry together invaded Normandy'; the invasion failed. No border change.
wars.note: The page gives no separate date for the battle itself.

wars.name: Battle of Varaville
wars.outcome: 'Duke William launched a sudden attack and defeated them'; no border change.
wars.note: The page does not explicitly date the battle; it mentions King Henry's 1057 summons.

wars.name: Norman conquest of Maine
wars.outcome: 'William invaded Maine in force in 1063' and 'controlled the county by the beginning of 1064'; the Angevin hold on Maine ends.
wars.note: Not an article title. Le Mans revolted in 1069 and expelled the Normans in 1070.

certainty.note: No page opened gives a treaty or surveyed frontier for Anjou; the county is described as 'roughly co-extensive with the diocese of Angers'. The Touraine and Maine frontiers moved with each conquest (1044, 1051, 1063, 1110) and are approximate.

notes: Pages: 5 of 5 budgeted (the Alençon page was read for the Normandy dossier and reused here). Cliopatria rows: (1) the County row has two lives, 990-1125 and 1294-1332, with a 168-year gap that the pages do not leave: the same polygon is the Angevins row 1126-1146 (own wikidata), then the Angevin Empire to 1209 (eu-11), then the royal domain, then the Capetian House of Anjou's land from August 1246 ('King Louis IX gave it as an appanage to his brother Charles, Count of Provence'; the House row starts 1250). The dossier is one state with a dormant span 1126-1289 (ledger merge 1126, gain 1290); the Angevins dossier (eu-10) and Angevin Empire dossier (eu-11) draw the land. If the orchestrator wants two states, split at 1294 and treat the Valois county as a new slug. (2) 861-989: the page dates the first count to 861 (Robert the Strong) and Fulk the Black from 21 July 987; the dossier starts at Cliopatria's 990 so as not to draw a county inside the West Franks row. (3) Saumur (1026) and Chinon (1044) are in the 990 shape too early: corrected. (4) Cliopatria draws Touraine two years late (1046), Maine five years late (1056) and the loss of Maine in 1066 (page 1063). (5) The 1294 shape holds Anjou and Maine only (dowry) with 11 unexplained scattered cells; Touraine, which Philip II conquered in 1204 (Maine page), is out. (6) The row ends in 1332 but the page reunites the county with the crown on 1 April 1328; the infobox gives John de Valois (1332-1360) and the duchy from 1360. Not covered: the Gâtinais ceded to Philip I (undated, 1068-1109), Loudun in fief from Aquitaine (undated), the 1081 homage of Robert Curthose for Maine, Geoffrey V's conquest of Normandy (1144) and Henry II's grant to his son (1168) because those are the Angevin Empire's. The Geoffrey II page puts the Domfront siege in winter 1052 and the Normans' History page puts the end of the Passais campaign in 1050: the Alençon and Domfront contest is 1049-1052 here and 1049-1050 in duchy-of-normandy. Counterparts needing dossiers: lord of Saumur (page silent); the rest (county-of-blois, county-of-maine, duchy-of-aquitaine, duchy-of-normandy, angevins, capetian-house-of-anjou, kingdom-of-france) exist or belong to other eu-10 parts. Gazetteer: Saumur, Chinon, Alençon, Domfront have no place entries; coordinates are used.
